cues: Welcome to the complete visual guide to writing the perfect prompt for Claude.
Prepared by Sara Salem.
In this video, you'll learn what makes a prompt great, and how to build one step by step — using the techniques recommended by Anthropic, the team that builds Claude.
Let's start with a simple comparison.
A weak prompt is short and vague, like: write something about marketing. Claude has to guess the audience, the length, the tone, and the goal — so the result is generic.
A great prompt is clear and specific. It explains the task, the context, the audience, and the format you want. Claude doesn't have to guess — so the result fits your needs on the first try.
Here's a helpful rule: imagine giving your prompt to a smart new colleague who knows nothing about your project. If they would be confused, Claude probably will be too.
A great prompt is built from a few key ingredients. Let's look at each one.
The role tells Claude who to be — for example, an experienced financial analyst, or a patient teacher.
The context explains the background: who the work is for, why it matters, and what Claude needs to know.
The task is the exact thing you want done, stated clearly and directly.
Examples show Claude what a great answer looks like.
The format describes how the output should look — its length, structure, and style.
And constraints set the boundaries: what to include, what to avoid, and any rules to follow.
Writing a great prompt is not a one-time event. It's a cycle.
First, define what success looks like.
Second, draft your prompt, using the ingredients we just covered.
Third, test it on real examples, and read the results carefully.
And fourth, refine it. Fix what didn't work, and test again — until the results are consistently great.
Now let's build a prompt, step by step. Step one: define success before you write anything.
Start with the goal. What should this prompt achieve?
Then the audience. Who will read or use the result?
Next, the output. What exactly should Claude produce — an email, a table, a summary, or code?
Then decide your success criteria. How will you judge whether a response is good?
And finally, collect a few test cases — real inputs you'll use to check the prompt.
Step two: be clear, direct, and specific. Let's turn a weak prompt into a strong one.
First, state the task precisely — here, a 150-word announcement for a new budgeting app.
Then add context, and explain why. Telling Claude the purpose helps it make better decisions.
Name the audience — in this case, busy small-business owners.
And describe the output: what to include, and the tone to use. The more specific you are, the better the result.
Step three: give Claude a role.
Using a system prompt, you can tell Claude who it should be — for example: you are a senior financial analyst at a growing company.
A role helps Claude use the right expertise, vocabulary, and level of detail.
It also shapes the tone — a legal reviewer is precise and careful, while a teacher is warm and encouraging.
Choose a role that matches the task, and be specific about the expertise you need.
Step four: structure your prompt with XML tags.
When a prompt has several parts, wrap each part in its own tag — like instructions, document, and examples. This keeps everything clearly separated.
Put long documents inside their own tags, near the top of the prompt, and place your question at the end.
You can also ask Claude to use tags in its answer — for example, putting the final answer inside answer tags, so it's easy to find and reuse.
There are no special magic tag names. Just use clear, consistent names that make sense.
Step five: show Claude examples. This is one of the most powerful techniques.
Examples show Claude exactly what you want — the format, the tone, and the level of detail.
As this illustrative chart shows, adding a few good examples usually makes the output much more consistent.
Anthropic recommends using about three to five examples, and making them diverse, so they cover different cases.
Wrap each one in example tags, so Claude can clearly tell examples apart from instructions.
Step six: let Claude think before it answers. For complex tasks, this improves accuracy.
Level one is basic: simply ask Claude to think step by step.
Level two is guided: list the specific steps you want Claude to think through — for example, first identify the key risks, then compare the options.
Level three is structured: ask Claude to write its reasoning inside thinking tags, and its final result inside answer tags. You can also turn on extended thinking, for Claude's deepest reasoning.
Thinking takes a little more time, but for analysis, math, and complex decisions, it's well worth it.
Step seven: break complex tasks into a chain of prompts.
Instead of asking for everything at once, split the work into focused stages. First, research the topic.
Next, create an outline.
Then, write the draft.
After that, review it against your criteria.
And finally, polish it. Each prompt's output becomes the next prompt's input — so every step gets Claude's full attention.
Step eight: test and iterate. This is what turns a good prompt into a great one.
Run your prompt on all of your test cases, and score each result against your success criteria.
Track the results for every version of your prompt.
In this illustrative example, each round of improvements raises the pass rate, and reduces the number of failures.
Study the failures closely. Each one tells you exactly what to clarify, add, or remove next.
Let's put it all together, in one complete prompt template.
It starts with the role, and the context — who Claude is, and why this task matters.
Then come the instructions, clearly numbered, and wrapped in their own tags.
Next, the examples and the input data, each in its own section.
And finally, the output format — telling Claude exactly how to structure its answer. You can reuse this template for almost any task.
You don't have to do it all by hand. The Claude Console includes tools that help you write better prompts.
The prompt generator creates a strong first draft from a simple description of your task.
The prompt improver takes an existing prompt, and makes it clearer and more structured.
Templates and variables let you reuse the same prompt with different inputs.
And the evaluation tool lets you run your prompt on many test cases, and compare the results side by side.
Here are six common mistakes to avoid.
One: being too vague. Always say exactly what you want.
Two: leaving out context. Explain who it's for, and why.
Three: only saying what not to do. Tell Claude what to do instead.
Four: cramming everything into one giant request. Split complex work into steps.
Five: forgetting the format. Describe how the answer should look.
And six: never testing. Always check your prompt on real examples.
With these skills, you can build great prompts for almost any task. Here are some ideas.
Professional emails, business reports, and meeting summaries.
Code reviews, data analysis, and research briefs.
Lesson plans, and marketing copy — each with its own reusable template.
Let's recap in one line: clear, structured, tested.
A perfect prompt is clear about the task, structured with context and examples, and tested on real cases — so Claude delivers great results, every time.
